title: Light — Reflection and Refraction
short: Ray diagrams, mirror and lens formulas, magnification and power.
lede: Six standard ray diagrams unlock every numerical in this chapter. Learn the sign convention once and the rest is substitution.
lens: **3–4 marks.** One ray diagram, one numerical on the mirror or lens formula, and one question on magnification or power.
Case-based questions give a practical situation — a dentist's mirror, a vehicle's rear-view mirror, a torch reflector — and ask which mirror is used and why.
concepts: **1. Reflection.** Light travelling in a straight line bounces back on striking a polished surface. **Laws of reflection:** the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. A **plane mirror** always forms a virtual, erect image, the same size as the object, at the same distance behind the mirror, and laterally inverted.

**2. Spherical mirrors.** **Concave** (converging, reflecting surface curves inwards) and **convex** (diverging). Key points: **P** (pole), **C** (centre of curvature), **F** (principal focus, midway between P and C), **R = 2f**. Aperture is the diameter of the reflecting surface.

head: Object position (concave mirror)
Image position
Nature and size
rows: Between P and F, behind mirror

concepts: **3. Refraction.** The bending of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium into another, caused by the change in its speed. Light bends **toward** the normal going from a rarer to a denser medium and **away** from the normal going the other way. It does not bend when it strikes the surface normally. Laws: (i) the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; (ii) **Snell's law** — the ratio sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media; this constant is the **refractive index**.

**4. Refractive index.** `n = c/v` (speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in the medium); it has no unit. Relative refractive index `n21 = n2/n1 = v1/v2`. Air ≈ 1.0003, water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.42 — diamond's high value gives it brilliance through total internal reflection.

**5. Lenses.** **Convex** (converging, thicker at the centre) and **concave** (diverging). A convex lens forms a real, inverted image for objects beyond F, and a **virtual, erect, magnified** image when the object is between F and the optical centre (this is why it is used as a magnifying glass). A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image.

**6. Power.** `P = 1/f` where f is in **metres**; the unit is the **dioptre (D)**. Convex lens power is positive, concave lens power negative. Powers of lenses in contact add up: `P = P1 + P2 + P3`. Prescriptions read +2.0 D (convex, for hypermetropia) or −1.5 D (concave, for myopia).
formulas: Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
R = 2f
Magnification m = h'/h = −v/u  (mirror)   and  m = h'/h = v/u  (lens)
Power P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre (D)
tricks: - **Sign convention:** distances measured against the direction of the incident light (to the left of the pole) are negative. Object distance **u is always negative**. For a concave mirror **f is negative**; for a convex mirror and a convex lens **f is positive**; a concave lens has negative f.
- **Nature from the sign of v:** for a mirror, negative v = real image (in front); positive v = virtual (behind). For a lens, positive v = real (on the other side); negative v = virtual (same side).
- **'Convex mirror = always virtual, erect, diminished'** — the reason it is used as a rear-view mirror, giving a wider field of view.
mistakes: - Using the mirror formula for a lens. Lens formula has **−v** and **+u** in the same form: `1/v − 1/u = 1/f`.
- Forgetting to convert f from cm to m before computing power. f = 20 cm must be written as **0.2 m**.
- Dropping the negative sign of m for a real, inverted image.
- Drawing the ray diagram without arrowheads on the rays and without marking C, F and P.

qa.q: State the mirror formula and the SI unit of the power of a lens.
qa.a: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. The SI unit of power is the **dioptre (D)**, equal to 1 m⁻¹.

qa.q: Why is a convex mirror preferred as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
qa.a: Because it always gives an erect, virtual and diminished image, and it has a wider field of view than a plane mirror, so the driver can see a much larger area of the traffic behind.

qa.q: A lens of power −4.0 D is placed in the path of light. Find its focal length and identify it.
qa.a: P = 1/f, so f = 1/(−4.0) = −0.25 m = −25 cm. Negative focal length means it is a **concave (diverging) lens**.

qa.q: Define the principal focus of a concave mirror and relate it to the radius of curvature.
qa.a: The principal focus is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (or appear to meet) after reflection. For a spherical mirror the focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature, so f = R/2.

qa.q: An object 4 cm high is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image.
a: So **v = −37.5 cm** — the image forms 37.5 cm in front of the mirror, hence real and inverted.
m = −v/u = −(−37.5)/(−25) = −1.5, so h' = −1.5 × 4 = **−6 cm**: the image is 6 cm tall, inverted, and magnified.

qa.q: Draw a ray diagram for an object placed between C and F of a concave mirror and state the nature of the image.
a: Draw the principal axis with P, F and C marked. Place the object (an arrow) between C and F.
Ray 1: parallel to the axis, reflected through F. Ray 2: through F, reflected parallel to the axis. (A third ray through C retraces its path.)
The rays meet **beyond C**, so the image is **real, inverted and magnified**. This is the arrangement used in a shaving or makeup mirror when the object is close.

qa.q: A student finds the power of a lens of focal length 20 cm as P = 1/f = 1/20 = 0.05 D. Find the mistake and give the correct power. What type of lens is it?
a: Mistake: the focal length must be in **metres** for power in dioptres. f = 20 cm = 0.2 m.
The focal length is positive, so the power is positive: it is a **convex** (converging) lens.

qa.q: A dentist uses a concave mirror of focal length 2 cm to see an enlarged, erect image of a tooth. At what distance from the mirror should the tooth be held for an image three times as large? Where is the image?
a: An erect, magnified image means m = +3, so v = −3u (with the sign convention).
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives 1/(−3u) + 1/u = 2/(3u) = 1/(−2), so u = −4/3 cm.
The tooth must be held about **1.33 cm** in front of the mirror. The image distance is v = −3u = +4 cm: a virtual image 4 cm behind the mirror.

qa.q: An object 5 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.
a: Using the lens formula 1/f = 1/v − 1/u with f = +20 cm and u = −30 cm:
Magnification m = v/u = 60/(−30) = −2, so h₂ = m × h₁ = −2 × 5 = −10 cm.
The image is real, inverted and twice the size, formed 60 cm on the other side of the lens.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A student places a candle 40 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm and obtains a sharp image on a screen.

(a) Where is the image formed?
(b) State its nature and its size relative to the object.
(c) What is the power of the lens?
a: (a) Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f gives 1/v = 1/20 − 1/40 = 1/40, so v = **+40 cm** (on the other side of the lens).
(b) m = v/u = 40/(−40) = −1, so the image is real, inverted and **the same size** as the object (the object is at 2F).

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A coin lies at the bottom of an empty opaque cup, just out of sight. When water is poured gently into the cup, the coin becomes visible.

(a) Name the phenomenon.
(b) Explain why the coin becomes visible.
(c) How does a ray bend as it passes from water into air?
a: (a) Refraction of light.
(b) Rays from the coin bend as they leave the water for the air, so they now reach the eye over the rim of the cup and the coin appears raised.
(c) Going from the denser water into the rarer air, the ray bends **away from the normal**.

qa.q: State the sign convention used for spherical mirrors and lenses, and apply it to a concave mirror.
a: All distances are measured from the pole (mirror) or the optical centre (lens).
Distances measured in the direction of the incident light are positive and those against it are negative; heights above the principal axis are positive and those below are negative.
In practice the object distance u is always negative, the focal length of a concave mirror and of a concave lens is negative, and that of a convex mirror and a convex lens is positive.

qa.q: State the laws of refraction and solve: light enters from air into glass (n = 1.5) with an angle of incidence of 30°. Find the angle of refraction and the speed of light in glass.
a: **Laws:** (i) the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane; (ii) for a given pair of media and a given colour, sin i / sin r is constant (Snell's law).
**Angle of refraction:** sin r = sin i / n = 0.5/1.5 = 0.3333, so r ≈ **19.5°** — the ray bends toward the normal.

qa.q: An object 5 cm high is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, nature and size of the image.
a: Sign convention: u = −20 cm and f = +10 cm for a convex mirror.
Mirror formula: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20, so v = **+20/3 ≈ +6.7 cm** (behind the mirror).
Magnification m = −v/u = −(20/3)/(−20) = +1/3.
Image height h′ = m × h = (1/3) × 5 ≈ **+1.7 cm**.
The image is virtual, erect and diminished, formed behind the mirror between the pole and the focus.

mcq.q: The magnification produced by a rear-view mirror fitted in vehicles is: (a) less than one (b) more than one (c) equal to one (d) more than one or less than one depending on the position of the object
mcq.a: **(a) less than one.** A convex mirror always forms a diminished, virtual and erect image.

mcq.q: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get a real image of the same size? (a) at F (b) at 2F (c) at infinity (d) between F and 2F
mcq.a: **(b) at 2F** — the image forms at 2F on the other side, real, inverted and of the same size.

mcq.q: The refractive index of water is 1.33. The speed of light in water is: (a) 3 × 10⁸ m/s (b) 2.26 × 10⁸ m/s (c) 1.33 × 10⁸ m/s (d) 4 × 10⁸ m/s

A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms a real image of the same size as the object. The object is placed at: (a) 15 cm from the mirror  (b) 30 cm from the mirror  (c) 45 cm from the mirror  (d) 7.5 cm from the mirror
mcq.a: **(b) 30 cm from the mirror.** A real image of the same size is formed when the object is at the centre of curvature, C = 2f = 30 cm.

mcq.q: The lens formula is: (a) 1/v + 1/u = 1/f  (b) 1/v − 1/u = 1/f  (c) 1/u − 1/v = 1/f  (d) v − u = f
mcq.a: **(b) 1/v − 1/u = 1/f.** With the Cartesian sign convention, the lens formula is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; the mirror formula has + between 1/v and 1/u.

mcq.q: The power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm is: (a) +2 D  (b) −2 D  (c) +0.5 D  (d) −0.5 D
mcq.a: **(a) +2 D.** P = 1/f in metres = 1/0.5 = +2 D; a converging lens always has positive power.

mcq.q: Which mirror always forms an erect and diminished image? (a) plane  (b) concave  (c) convex  (d) parabolic
mcq.a: **(c) convex.** Its image is always virtual, erect and smaller, which is why it is used as a rear-view mirror.

mcq.q: When a ray of light goes from glass into air, it: (a) bends towards the normal  (b) bends away from the normal  (c) does not bend  (d) is totally absorbed
mcq.a: **(b) bends away from the normal.** Moving from a denser to a rarer medium, the ray speeds up and bends away from the normal.

mcq.q: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed: (a) 10 cm in front of the mirror  (b) 20 cm in front of the mirror  (c) 20 cm behind the mirror  (d) at infinity
mcq.a: **(b) 20 cm in front of the mirror.** The object is at C (2f = 20 cm), so the image is also at C, real, inverted and the same size. Mirror formula: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/20 = −1/20, v = −20 cm.

mcq.q: A ray of light enters a denser medium along the normal (angle of incidence 0°). It: (a) bends towards the normal  (b) bends away from the normal  (c) passes undeviated  (d) is totally reflected
mcq.a: **(c) passes undeviated.** Refraction changes the speed but there is no bending when the ray is along the normal, because sin 0° = 0 on both sides of Snell's law.

mcq.q: The image formed by a concave lens of a real object is always: (a) real and inverted  (b) virtual, erect and diminished  (c) virtual, erect and magnified  (d) real and magnified
mcq.a: **(b) virtual, erect and diminished.** A diverging lens forms the image between F₁ and the optical centre on the same side as the object, whatever the object distance.

trend: One ray diagram (concave mirror or convex lens) and one numerical using the mirror/lens formula with the magnification appear nearly every year; power and the sign of the focal length are common 1-mark items.
onepager: - Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, m = −v/u. Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u.
- u is always negative; concave mirror f negative; convex lens f positive.
- Convex mirror → always virtual, erect, diminished (rear-view mirror).
- P = 1/f in metres, in dioptres; powers add in contact.
- n = c/v; denser medium bends light toward the normal.
task: Using a concave mirror (or a spoon's inner surface) and a candle, find the focal length by focusing the sun or a distant window on a screen. Then place the candle at 2f and measure the image distance and size — check that v ≈ 2f and that the image is the same size and inverted.
steps: 1. Decide which **mirror or lens** is involved, then write down the sign convention you will use (Cartesian: distances measured from the pole/optical centre, left is negative).
2. List what is given as **u, v, f, R, h, h′** with their signs; convert everything to centimetres before substituting.

3. Substitute into the **mirror formula** 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (or the lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f) and solve. Do the arithmetic a second time — most lost marks here are arithmetic slips, not concept errors.

4. Interpret the sign of the answer: negative v means a real image in front, positive means virtual behind. Then state **size, nature and position** in one line, since the question usually asks for all three.

title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
short: Defects of vision, dispersion, atmospheric refraction and scattering.
lede: Four defects, four corrections, and four sky-colour reasons. Small chapter, guaranteed marks.
lens: **2–3 marks.** Myopia/hypermetropia with a labelled diagram is the single most repeated question in Physics.
The 'why is the sky blue / why is the sunrise red' question appears regularly as a 2-mark reasoning item.
concepts: **1. The eye as a camera.** **Cornea** — most of the refraction happens here. **Iris** — the dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the **pupil** and hence the amount of light entering. **Crystalline lens** — a convex lens of adjustable focal length; **ciliary muscles** change its curvature, so a clear image is formed on the **retina** for objects at all distances. This is the **power of accommodation**. The image on the retina is real and inverted; the optic nerve carries the signal to the brain. The **blind spot** is where the optic nerve leaves and there are no photoreceptors. **Least distance of distinct vision** = 25 cm for a normal adult eye; far point = infinity.

**2. Defects of vision.** **Myopia** (short sight) — the person sees near objects clearly but not distant ones; caused by excessive curvature of the lens or elongation of the eyeball; the image forms **in front of** the retina; corrected with a **concave lens**. **Hypermetropia** (long sight) — cannot see nearby objects clearly; image forms **behind** the retina; corrected with a **convex lens**. **Presbyopia** — the power of accommodation decreases with age; corrected with a **bifocal lens**.

**3. Dispersion.** The splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours (VIBGYOR) by a glass prism. Newton showed with two identical prisms, one inverted over the other, that white light is a mixture of colours. Red bends least, violet most, because different colours travel at different speeds in glass. **Rainbow formation:** refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection of sunlight by water droplets acting as tiny prisms — you see it with the sun behind you.

**4. Atmospheric refraction.** The refractive index of air decreases with altitude, so light from a star bends continuously as it enters the atmosphere. Effects: **stars twinkle** (the apparent position and brightness keep changing), **planets do not twinkle** (they are nearer and act as extended sources, so the variations average out), the **sun appears above the horizon about two minutes before actual sunrise and two minutes after sunset** (daylight is lengthened by about 4 minutes), and **stars appear slightly higher** than their true position.

**5. Scattering of light.** Fine particles scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths more strongly — the **Tyndall effect**. This explains the **blue colour of the sky**, the **reddish appearance of the sun at sunrise and sunset** (blue is scattered away over the long path, leaving red), the **white appearance of clouds** (large water droplets scatter all colours equally), and why **danger signals are red** (red scatters least and travels farthest through fog and smoke). At noon the sun looks white because the path through the atmosphere is short.
formulas: Power of a lens: P = 1/f (f in metres, P in dioptres)
Correction: myopia → concave (diverging) lens of negative power; hypermetropia → convex (converging) lens of positive power
Presbyopia → bifocal lens; astigmatism → cylindrical lens
Scattering intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ — shorter wavelength scatters far more
Refractive index and deviation: violet deviates most, red least
tricks: - **Myopia = image in front = concave lens.** *'My-o-pia → My oh, I can't see far → Concave.'*
- **Hypermetropia = image behind = convex lens.** *'Hyper → beyond → behind → convex.'*
- **VIBGYOR: red deviates least, violet most.** Same order explains the rainbow and the prism.
mistakes: - Drawing the corrective lens on the wrong side of the eye diagram, or labelling the image position incorrectly (in front for myopia, behind for hypermetropia).
- Saying 'the sky is blue because it reflects the sea'. It is **scattering** by air molecules.
- Explaining twinkling as 'stars burning unevenly'. It is **atmospheric refraction**.
- Forgetting that **presbyopia** is due to the weakening of the ciliary muscles and loss of flexibility of the lens, not a change in the eyeball's length.

qa.q: Name the part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering it, and the least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye.
qa.a: The iris (which adjusts the size of the pupil); 25 cm.

qa.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets do not?
qa.a: Starlight passes through layers of air of changing refractive index, so its path keeps changing slightly and the apparent brightness and position fluctuate — the star twinkles. Planets are much nearer and behave as a collection of many point sources, so the fluctuations from different parts cancel out and the total light remains steady.

qa.q: Why does the sun appear reddish early in the morning?
qa.a: Because near the horizon sunlight travels through a much thicker layer of air. The shorter blue wavelengths are scattered away, and mainly the longer red wavelengths reach our eyes, so the sun looks red. At noon the path is short, little blue light is scattered, and the sun looks white.

qa.q: What is the power of accommodation of the eye?
qa.a: It is the ability of the eye lens to change its focal length — by the action of the ciliary muscles — so that both near and distant objects are focused sharply on the retina. In a normal eye the near point is about 25 cm and the far point is infinity.

qa.q: What is myopia? State its two causes and its correction.
a: Myopia (short-sightedness) is the defect in which a person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly; the image of a distant object forms **in front of the retina**.
**Causes:** (i) excessive curvature of the eye lens, (ii) elongation of the eyeball.
**Correction:** a **concave lens** of suitable power, which diverges the light so that the image is formed exactly on the retina.

qa.q: Explain the formation of a rainbow in the sky.
a: After rain, tiny water droplets remain suspended in the air and act as small glass prisms.

Sunlight entering a droplet is first **refracted and dispersed** into its constituent colours, then undergoes **total internal reflection** at the inner surface of the droplet, and is **refracted again** as it leaves.
Because different colours emerge at slightly different angles, the observer sees a coloured arc — a rainbow — with the sun always behind them.

qa.q: A student explains the twinkling of stars by saying, “Stars burn unevenly, so their brightness keeps changing.” Correct the explanation and say why planets do not twinkle.
a: Twinkling is caused by **atmospheric refraction**, not by the star burning unevenly.
Starlight passes through layers of air whose density and refractive index keep changing, so the star’s apparent position wobbles slightly and the amount of light entering the eye fluctuates.
A planet is much nearer and acts like a collection of many point sources; the fluctuations average out, so a planet does not twinkle.

qa.q: A student cannot see objects clearly beyond 80 cm. Name the defect, the type of corrective lens required, and calculate its power.
a: The far point is only 80 cm, so the student is **short-sighted (myopic)**.
A **concave** lens is needed; it must form a virtual image of a distant object at 80 cm, so f = −80 cm = −0.8 m.

qa.q: What is presbyopia? State its cause and how it is corrected.
a: Presbyopia is the loss of the eye's power of accommodation with age: the ciliary muscles weaken and the lens becomes less flexible.
As a result the near point recedes and reading or threading a needle becomes difficult.
It is corrected with converging (convex) spectacles; when a person has both myopia and presbyopia, bifocal lenses are used.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Rahul sees distant objects clearly but cannot read a book held at the normal distance of 25 cm.

(a) Name the defect.
(b) Give two possible causes.
(c) Name the corrective lens and explain how it helps.
a: (a) Hypermetropia (far-sightedness).
(b) The focal length of the eye lens is too long, or the eyeball is too short, so the image of a near object forms behind the retina.
(c) A **convex** lens: it converges the rays a little before they enter the eye, so the image forms on the retina.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism and forms a band of seven colours on a screen. When the same beam passes through a rectangular glass slab, no band of colours appears.

(a) Name the phenomenon seen with the prism.
(b) Which colour bends the most and which the least?
(c) Why does the rectangular slab not show it?
a: (a) Dispersion of white light.
(b) Violet bends the most and red the least.
(c) The opposite faces of a slab are parallel, so the colours spread on entering are brought back together on leaving, and emerge as white light again.

qa.q: Explain why the sky looks blue and the sun looks white at noon but red at sunrise.
a: Air molecules and fine particles scatter light of short wavelength much more strongly than long wavelength light (scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴).
Blue light is scattered the most, so light reaching the eye from all parts of the sky is rich in blue.
At noon the sun is overhead and its light crosses the shortest possible path, so very little blue is removed and the sun looks white.
Near sunrise and sunset the path through the atmosphere is much longer, most of the blue is scattered away, and the remaining direct light looks red.

qa.q: Explain atmospheric refraction and describe any three phenomena based on it.
a: **Atmospheric refraction** is the bending of light as it passes through layers of air of different densities; the refractive index of air decreases as we go up, so light from a celestial body bends gradually toward the normal.
**(1) Twinkling of stars:** the continuously changing refractive index makes the apparent position and brightness of a star fluctuate.

**(2) Advance of sunrise and delay of sunset:** light from the sun below the horizon is refracted toward the earth, so the sun becomes visible about two minutes before actual sunrise and remains visible about two minutes after sunset — the day is lengthened by about 4 minutes.
**(3) Apparent flattening of the sun's disc** at sunrise and sunset, and stars appearing slightly higher than their true position, are also caused by the same refraction.

qa.q: Describe how the human eye forms an image of an object and how it adjusts to see objects at different distances.
a: Light enters through the transparent cornea, which does most of the bending of light; the iris controls the size of the pupil and so the amount of light entering.
The eye lens focuses the light and forms a real, inverted image on the retina.
The retina contains light-sensitive cells that produce electrical signals, which the optic nerve carries to the brain; the brain interprets the image as erect.
For different distances, the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the lens, and so its focal length. This is called **accommodation**.
For nearby objects the lens becomes thicker (shorter focal length); for distant objects it becomes thinner.

mcq.q: The change in focal length of the eye lens is caused by the action of the: (a) pupil (b) retina (c) ciliary muscles (d) iris
mcq.a: **(c) ciliary muscles** — they change the curvature of the crystalline lens, giving the eye its power of accommodation.

mcq.q: The danger signals installed at the top of tall buildings are red because red light: (a) is scattered the most by smoke or fog (b) is scattered the least by smoke or fog (c) is absorbed the most (d) moves fastest in air
mcq.a: **(b) is scattered the least** — being of the longest wavelength, so it can be seen from a greater distance through fog or smoke.

mcq.q: A person cannot read a newspaper without glasses. He is probably suffering from: (a) myopia (b) hypermetropia (c) astigmatism (d) night blindness
mcq.a: **(b) hypermetropia** — difficulty in seeing near objects clearly, corrected with a convex lens.

mcq.q: The eye defect hypermetropia is corrected by using a: (a) concave lens  (b) cylindrical lens  (c) convex lens  (d) bifocal lens with a concave upper part
mcq.a: **(c) convex lens.** In hypermetropia the image forms behind the retina, so a converging (convex) lens is used.

mcq.q: The part of the eye that contains the light-sensitive cells is the: (a) cornea  (b) iris  (c) retina  (d) pupil
mcq.a: **(c) retina.** The retina holds the rods and cones that convert light into electrical signals.

mcq.q: The eye defect in which the far point is nearer than infinity is: (a) hypermetropia  (b) myopia  (c) presbyopia  (d) cataract
mcq.a: **(b) myopia.** Short-sightedness is corrected with a diverging (concave) lens.

mcq.q: The splitting of white light into its component colours is called: (a) scattering  (b) dispersion  (c) total internal reflection  (d) polarisation
mcq.a: **(b) dispersion.** Different wavelengths bend by different amounts inside a prism, so the colours separate.

mcq.q: Stars twinkle mainly because of: (a) atmospheric refraction  (b) dispersion  (c) reflection from clouds  (d) their own flickering
mcq.a: **(a) atmospheric refraction.** Moving layers of air of changing density bend the starlight by varying amounts, so its apparent position shifts rapidly.

mcq.q: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal vision is about: (a) 2.5 cm  (b) 25 cm  (c) 25 m  (d) infinity
mcq.a: **(b) 25 cm.** This is the near point; the far point of a normal eye is at infinity.

mcq.q: The clear sky appears blue because: (a) blue light is absorbed the most  (b) shorter wavelengths are scattered more by air molecules  (c) the sea reflects blue light upwards  (d) the atmosphere refracts blue light towards the eye
mcq.a: **(b) shorter wavelengths are scattered more by air molecules.** Fine particles scatter blue light far more than red, so scattered blue reaches the eye from every direction.

mcq.q: A student with myopia is prescribed a lens of power −2.0 D. The lens is: (a) convex, focal length 50 cm  (b) concave, focal length 50 cm  (c) concave, focal length 2 m  (d) convex, focal length 2 m
mcq.a: **(b) concave, focal length 50 cm.** f = 1/P = 1/(−2) m = −0.5 m; the negative sign means a concave (diverging) lens, which corrects myopia.

trend: One defect of vision with a labelled diagram is asked almost every year; the sky-blue / red-sunrise reasoning and the rainbow are the next most common.
onepager: - Myopia → image in front → concave lens. Hypermetropia → image behind → convex lens. Presbyopia → bifocal.
- Least distance of distinct vision 25 cm; far point infinity.
- Dispersion: red bends least, violet most; rainbow = refraction + dispersion + TIR in droplets.
- Twinkling, advance sunrise/delay sunset = atmospheric refraction. Blue sky, red sunrise = scattering.
task: Make a spectrum with a glass prism and a white screen, and mark the order of colours. Then hold a second identical prism inverted above the first and observe the recombination into white light — this is exactly Newton's experiment.
steps: 1. For a **defect of vision**, name it, say where the image forms (myopia: in front of the retina; hypermetropia: would form behind it), and quote the **correcting lens** — concave for myopia, convex for hypermetropia.
2. For a **dispersion** question, state that white light splits into seven colours because different wavelengths refract by different amounts — violet deviates most, red least.
3. For **scattering**, apply the inverse-fourth law: shorter wavelengths scatter far more, which is why the sky is blue and the sun looks red at sunrise and sunset.
4. End with the **everyday example** asked for — the apparent position of stars due to atmospheric refraction, or the rainbow after rain.

title: Electricity
short: Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, heating effect and power.
lede: The most numerical-heavy chapter in the paper. Three formulas cover everything; the rest is careful reading of the circuit.
lens: **3–4 marks.** A series or parallel circuit numerical is almost certain, plus one question on the heating effect or on power rating.
Case-based questions usually give a household circuit (parallel wiring) and ask why appliances are connected in parallel and what happens to the resistance.
concepts: **1. Electric current and potential difference.** Current `I = Q/t`, measured in **amperes** with an **ammeter** connected **in series**. Potential difference `V = W/Q`, measured in **volts** with a **voltmeter** connected **in parallel**; 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb. By convention current flows from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to the flow of electrons. A **cell** maintains the potential difference that drives the charge.

**2. Ohm's law.** At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends: `V = IR`. The **V–I graph** for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; its slope gives R. Resistance is the property that opposes the flow of current, `R = ρl/A`, measured in **ohms (Ω)** — it increases with length, decreases with area of cross-section, and depends on the material and temperature.

**3. Resistors in series.** The same current flows through each; total `R = R1 + R2 + R3`, which is **greater than the largest** individual resistance. Voltages divide in the ratio of the resistances. Series wiring is used when the total resistance must be increased, as in a decorative bulb string.

**4. Resistors in parallel.** The same potential difference is across each; `1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3`, and the total is **less than the smallest** individual resistance. This is why domestic appliances are connected in parallel — each gets the full supply voltage, each has its own switch, and the failure of one does not affect the others.

**5. Heating effect of current.** `H = I²Rt` (joules) — also written `H = VIt = V²t/R`. Applications: the **electric heater, geyser and iron** (high-resistance nichrome heating element), the **electric bulb** (tungsten filament, melting point 3380 °C, filled with argon and nitrogen so the filament does not oxidise), and the **electric fuse** (a wire of low melting point in series that melts if the current exceeds a safe value; ISI mark and rating such as 5 A). A **circuit breaker** and **earthing** (the metal body of an appliance connected to the earth) protect the user from electric shock.
formulas: I = Q/t ; 1 A = 1 C/s
V = W/Q ; 1 V = 1 J/C
V = IR ; R = ρl/A
Series: Rs = R1 + R2 + R3
Parallel: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3
H = I²Rt = VIt = V²t/R
P = VI = I²R = V²/R ; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
tricks: - **Series = same current, voltage divides. Parallel = same voltage, current divides.** Read that sentence before every circuit question.
- **Parallel resistance is always smaller** than the smallest resistor. If your answer is bigger, you have used the series formula.
- **Units for energy:** the board wants kWh for a household bill. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Always convert hours, not minutes.
mistakes: - Connecting the ammeter in parallel and the voltmeter in series in a circuit diagram — this is a marked error.
- Using `H = I²Rt` and then quoting the answer in kWh without converting joules.
- Forgetting that the resistance of the connecting wires and the ammeter is taken as zero, while the voltmeter has very high resistance.
- In the parallel formula, adding the resistances instead of the **reciprocals**, and not taking the reciprocal of the final sum.

qa.q: Define one ohm and name the device used to measure potential difference.
qa.a: One ohm is the resistance of a conductor when a potential difference of 1 volt across its ends produces a current of 1 ampere through it. Potential difference is measured with a **voltmeter**, connected in parallel.

qa.q: Why are the coils of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
qa.a: Because alloys have higher resistivity than the pure metals, so they produce more heat for the same current, and they do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures.

qa.q: An electric iron of rating 750 W, 220 V is used for 2 hours daily. Calculate the cost of using it for 30 days at ₹5 per unit.
a: Energy per day = P × t = 750 W × 2 h = 1500 Wh = **1.5 kWh**.
Energy for 30 days = 1.5 × 30 = **45 kWh** = 45 units.

qa.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel and not in series?
qa.a: In a parallel circuit every appliance gets the full supply voltage and works independently, so switching one off does not affect the others and a fault in one branch does not stop the rest — none of which is possible in a series circuit.

qa.q: State Ohm's law and draw the V–I graph for an ohmic conductor.
a: At constant temperature, the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends: V = IR, where R is the resistance.
The graph of V against I is a **straight line passing through the origin**; its slope (V/I) gives the resistance of the conductor.

qa.q: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
a: So **Rp = 1 Ω** — less than the smallest resistor (2 Ω), as expected for a parallel combination.

qa.q: A student finds the equivalent resistance of 6 Ω and 3 Ω connected in parallel as 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. Identify the mistake and find the correct value.
a: Mistake: resistances are added directly only in **series**. In parallel the reciprocals are added.
R = **2 Ω**, which is smaller than the smallest resistance (3 Ω), as it must be in a parallel combination.

qa.q: A copper wire has a resistance of 10 Ω. What will be the resistance of a wire of the same material that is twice as long and has half the area of cross-section?
a: Resistance R = ρl/A, so for a given material R is proportional to l/A.
New length = 2l and new area = A/2, so the new resistance = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4 × ρl/A.
New resistance = 4 × 10 = **40 Ω**.

qa.q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel and the combination is joined to a 6 V battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the current drawn from the battery.
a: Current I = V/R = 6/3 = 2 A.
Check: the branch currents are 6/4 = 1.5 A and 6/12 = 0.5 A, which add to 2 A. Note the equivalent resistance is less than the smaller resistor.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A 12 V battery is connected in series to resistors of 4 Ω and 2 Ω, an ammeter, and a voltmeter across the 4 Ω resistor.

(a) Find the current in the circuit.
(b) Find the voltmeter reading.
(c) Find the heat produced in the 2 Ω resistor in 10 s.
a: (a) Total resistance = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω, so I = V/R = 12/6 = **2 A**.
(b) V across 4 Ω = IR = 2 × 4 = **8 V**.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A household uses three 40 W bulbs for 5 hours daily, a 1 kW heater for 2 hours daily and a 100 W fan for 10 hours daily.

(a) Find the electrical energy used per day in kWh.
(b) How many units are used in 30 days?
(c) What is the monthly cost at Rs 7 per unit?
a: (a) Bulbs: 0.12 kW × 5 h = 0.6 kWh; heater: 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh; fan: 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh. Total = **3.6 kWh** per day.

qa.q: A 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb are both rated at 220 V. Which has the higher resistance, and what current does each draw?
a: Using R = V²/P: R₁₀₀ = 220²/100 = 484 Ω and R₆₀ = 220²/60 ≈ 806.7 Ω.
So the 60 W bulb has the higher resistance — the lower-power bulb resists the current more.
Currents: I = P/V, so the 100 W bulb draws 100/220 ≈ 0.45 A and the 60 W bulb draws 60/220 ≈ 0.27 A.

qa.q: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 20 V battery. Find the total resistance, the current, the potential difference across each resistor, and the heat produced in the 4 Ω resistor in 1 minute.
a: **Total resistance** Rs = 4 + 6 = **10 Ω**.
**Current** I = V/R = 20/10 = **2 A** — the same through both resistors.
**Potential differences:** across 4 Ω, V = 2 × 4 = **8 V**; across 6 Ω, V = 2 × 6 = **12 V**. (8 + 12 = 20 V ✓)
**Heat in the 4 Ω resistor** H = I²Rt = (2)² × 4 × 60 = **960 J**.

qa.q: State Joule’s law of heating. Derive the expression H = I²Rt and give three applications of the heating effect of current.
a: Joule’s law: the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current, to its resistance and to the time for which the current flows.
Derivation: charge Q = It flows through potential difference V, so work done (energy converted) W = VQ = VIt.
By Ohm’s law V = IR, so H = (IR) × I × t = **I²Rt**.
Applications: electric heater, iron and toaster (coils of high-resistance alloy); the fuse (it melts when the current is too high); the filament of an electric bulb (tungsten glows white-hot).

mcq.q: The least resistance that can be obtained by combining 2 Ω, 4 Ω, 1 Ω and 100 Ω is: (a) more than 100 Ω (b) less than 1 Ω (c) 107 Ω (d) between 2 Ω and 100 Ω
mcq.a: **(b) less than 1 Ω.** Connecting all four in parallel gives an equivalent resistance smaller than the smallest individual resistance, 1 Ω.

mcq.q: Two wires of the same material and length but different cross-sectional areas are compared. The thicker wire has: (a) more resistance (b) less resistance (c) the same resistance (d) no resistance
mcq.a: **(b) less resistance**, since R = ρl/A and a larger area of cross-section reduces the resistance.

mcq.q: The commercial unit of electrical energy is: (a) joule (b) watt (c) kilowatt-hour (d) volt
mcq.a: **(c) kilowatt-hour (kWh)**, equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J, and commonly called a 'unit'.

mcq.q: The electric power consumed by a resistor R connected to a potential difference V is given by: (a) P = V²/R  (b) P = VR²  (c) P = R/V²  (d) P = V/R²
mcq.a: **(a) P = V²/R.** P = VI and I = V/R, so P = V × (V/R) = V²/R.

mcq.q: The SI unit of resistivity is: (a) ohm (Ω)  (b) ohm metre (Ω m)  (c) ohm per metre (Ω/m)  (d) siemens (S)
mcq.a: **(b) ohm metre (Ω m).** From R = ρl/A, ρ = RA/l, whose unit is Ω × m²/m = Ω m.

mcq.q: The resistance of a wire doubles when: (a) its length is doubled  (b) its area of cross-section is doubled  (c) its length is halved  (d) its diameter is doubled
mcq.a: **(a) its length is doubled.** R ∝ l/A; doubling the area halves R, doubling the diameter reduces R to a quarter.

mcq.q: One kilowatt hour equals: (a) 3.6 × 10⁶ J  (b) 3.6 × 10³ J  (c) 360 J  (d) 6 × 10µ J
An ammeter is connected in a circuit: (a) in series  (b) in parallel  (c) across the supply  (d) either way
mcq.a: **(a) in series.** It has very low resistance so it does not change the current; a voltmeter is connected in parallel.

mcq.q: A 12 V battery drives a current of 2 A through a resistor. The resistance of the resistor is: (a) 24 Ω  (b) 6 Ω  (c) 0.17 Ω  (d) 14 Ω
Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is: (a) 18 Ω  (b) 6 Ω  (c) 2 Ω  (d) 3 Ω
mcq.a: **(c) 2 Ω.** 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 3/6, so R = 2 Ω — equal resistors in parallel give R/n.

mcq.q: A 100 W bulb is used for 10 hours every day. The electrical energy it consumes in 30 days is: (a) 3 kWh  (b) 30 kWh  (c) 300 kWh  (d) 3000 kWh
mcq.a: **(b) 30 kWh.** Energy = power × time = 0.1 kW × 10 h × 30 = 30 kWh, i.e. 30 units.

trend: A series/parallel circuit numerical appears every year, and the heating-effect formula with a household energy-bill calculation is the most repeated 3–5 mark question in Physics.
onepager: - V = IR; R = ρl/A; series Rs = R1+R2+R3; parallel 1/Rp = 1/R1+1/R2+1/R3.
- Series: same current. Parallel: same voltage.
- H = I²Rt = VIt = V²t/R; P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
- 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.
- Fuse: low melting point, in series, protects from overcurrent; earthing prevents shock.
task: Wire two 1.5 V cells in series with a 5 Ω and a 10 Ω resistor in series, and measure the current with an ammeter and the potential difference across each resistor with a voltmeter. Verify V = IR for each resistor and that the voltages add up to the battery voltage.
steps: 1. Sketch the circuit in words and decide whether the resistors are in **series** (same current, Rs = R1 + R2 …) or **parallel** (same voltage, 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 …).
2. Write down **Ohm's law** V = IR for the part of the circuit you are solving, and keep the units straight — current in amperes, potential difference in volts, resistance in ohms.
3. For heating, use **H = I²Rt** when the current is known and H = VIt when the voltage is known; state the power as P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
4. Check the **physical sense** of your answer: in series, total resistance must exceed the largest single resistor; in parallel, it must be smaller than the smallest.

title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
short: Field patterns, the three hand rules, the motor and the generator.
lede: Rule-heavy but very short. Get Fleming's two rules and the three hand rules straight and the questions are mechanical.
lens: **2–3 marks.** Fleming's left-hand and right-hand rules and the difference between AC and DC are asked repeatedly.
Domestic circuits and the role of the earth wire or fuse are a favourite case-based topic.
concepts: **1. Magnetic field and field lines.** A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet in which its force can be detected. Field lines are **closed continuous curves** — outside a bar magnet they run from the **north to the south pole** and inside from south to north. Two field lines never intersect (that would mean two directions of force at one point). The relative strength is shown by how close the lines are.

**2. Field around a current-carrying conductor.** A straight wire produces **concentric circles** around it; increasing the current or decreasing the distance from the wire strengthens the field. A circular loop produces concentric circles that are nearly parallel at the centre; a **solenoid** produces a field like a bar magnet, with one end behaving as the north pole — this is how an **electromagnet** is made. **Oersted's experiment** showed that a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire is deflected, so an electric current produces a magnetic field.

**3. Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.** A conductor carrying current placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is **maximum when the conductor is perpendicular** to the field. **Fleming's left-hand rule:** stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular; if the **forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field** and the **middle finger in the direction of the current**, then the **thumb gives the direction of the force** (motion). This is the principle of the **electric motor**.

**4. The electric motor.** A rectangular coil placed between the poles of a magnet; when current flows, the coil experiences a torque and rotates. The **split ring (commutator)** reverses the direction of current in the coil every half rotation, so the rotation continues in one direction. Uses: fans, mixers, washing machines, pumps. **Electromagnetic induction:** when the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a current is induced in it — **Fleming's right-hand rule** gives the direction of the induced current (thumb = motion, forefinger = field, middle finger = induced current).

**5. The electric generator.** It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. A **DC generator** uses a split-ring commutator and gives current in one direction; an **AC generator** uses two slip rings and the current reverses direction periodically. In India, AC has a frequency of **50 Hz**, so its direction changes **100 times in one second**.

**6. Domestic electric circuits.** Live wire (red, 220 V), neutral (black, 0 V) and earth wire (green, connected to a metal plate deep in the earth). Appliances with metallic bodies — geysers, irons, toasters — are earthed so that leakage current flows to the earth instead of through the user. **Short circuit** — live and neutral touch, resistance becomes almost zero, current rises enormously. **Overloading** — too many appliances on one circuit. **Fuse** and **MCB** protect the circuit; separate circuits of 15 A and 5 A are provided.
formulas: Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = B I L (for a conductor perpendicular to the field)
Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field, Second finger = Current, Thumb = Force (motion)
Fleming's right-hand rule: for induced current in a generator
Domestic supply in India: 220 V, 50 Hz AC — live (red/brown), neutral (black/blue), earth (green)
Fuse rating: choose a fuse whose rating is just above the current the appliance draws
tricks: - **Left hand = Motor, Right hand = Generator.** *'M' for motor and 'M' is in the word 'Motion' — but remember: the **left** hand has the thumb as Force, so Motor = Left.*
- **Field lines never intersect** — the standard one-mark reason question.
- **AC 50 Hz changes direction 100 times a second** (twice per cycle).
mistakes: - Saying field lines run from south to north *outside* a magnet. Outside it is **north to south**.
- Mixing up Fleming's left-hand rule (force/motor) with the right-hand rule (induced current/generator).
- Stating that the split ring makes the motor faster. It **reverses the current** every half rotation so that rotation continues in one direction.
- Forgetting that the earth wire is connected to the **metallic body** of the appliance, not to the live wire.

qa.q: State Fleming's right-hand rule.
qa.a: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the thumb in the direction of motion of the conductor, the middle finger gives the direction of the induced current.

qa.q: Why do two magnetic field lines never intersect each other?
qa.a: Because at the point of intersection there would be two directions of the magnetic field for a single point, which is impossible — a compass needle placed there could not point in two directions at once.

qa.q: Differentiate between an AC generator and a DC generator.
qa.a: An **AC generator** uses two complete slip rings, and the current it produces reverses direction periodically (50 Hz in India). A **DC generator** uses a split-ring commutator, so although the current in the coil reverses, the current in the external circuit always flows in one direction.

qa.q: State the rule used to find the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
qa.a: Right-hand thumb rule: imagine holding the conductor in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the current; the direction in which your fingers curl around the conductor is the direction of the magnetic field lines, which are concentric circles around the wire.

qa.q: Explain the principle and working of an electric motor.
a: **Principle:** a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
**Working:** a rectangular coil ABCD is placed between the poles of a magnet. When current flows, one arm is pushed up and the other down, so the coil rotates.
The **split-ring commutator** reverses the direction of current in the coil after every half rotation, so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.
**Uses:** electric fans, mixers, washing machines and pumps.

qa.q: What is electromagnetic induction? Describe an activity to demonstrate it.
a: When the magnetic field linked with a coil changes, a current is induced in the coil — this is electromagnetic induction.

**Activity:** connect a galvanometer to a coil. Push a bar magnet's north pole into the coil and the galvanometer needle deflects momentarily in one direction; pull it out and it deflects in the opposite direction; hold it still inside and there is no deflection.
The deflection shows that a current is induced only when the magnetic flux through the coil is changing, i.e. only while the magnet is in relative motion.

qa.q: A student draws the field lines of a bar magnet as coming out of the south pole and entering the north pole outside the magnet. Correct the statement and state two properties of magnetic field lines.
a: Outside the magnet, field lines run from the **north pole to the south pole**; inside the magnet they run from south to north, so each line is a closed loop.
Property 1: the lines are closed curves that never cross one another.
Property 2: the field is strongest where the lines are closest together, i.e. near the poles.

qa.q: A coil of wire is connected to a galvanometer. When a bar magnet is pushed into the coil, the needle deflects. What happens (i) when the magnet is held still inside the coil, (ii) when it is pulled out, and (iii) how can the deflection be increased?
a: (i) No deflection: a current is induced only while the magnetic field linked with the coil is **changing**.
(ii) The needle deflects in the opposite direction, because the change in the field is reversed.
(iii) Move the magnet faster, use a stronger magnet or use a coil with more turns. This is electromagnetic induction.

qa.q: How does the strength of the magnetic field at the centre of a current-carrying circular coil depend on the current, the number of turns and the radius of the coil?
a: It is directly proportional to the current flowing through the coil.
It is directly proportional to the number of turns, because the field of each turn adds up.
It is inversely proportional to the radius of the coil, so a smaller coil gives a stronger field. This is the principle behind electromagnets and solenoids.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A student winds insulated copper wire round an iron nail and connects the ends to a battery. The nail picks up small iron pins, but drops them when the battery is disconnected.

(a) Name this device.
(b) Why does it hold the pins only while the current flows?
(c) State two ways to make it stronger.
a: (a) An **electromagnet** (a solenoid with a soft iron core).
(b) The current-carrying coil magnetises the iron core; soft iron loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops, so the pins fall.
(c) Increase the number of turns of the coil, or increase the current (a soft iron core also strengthens it).

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A socket in a house is protected by a 5 A fuse, and the supply is 220 V.

(a) Find the current drawn by a 1 kW heater.
(b) Will the fuse blow if a 2 kW geyser is plugged in instead? Justify.
(c) State the purpose of the fuse and of the earth wire.
a: (a) I = P/V = 1000/220 ≈ **4.5 A**, which is below 5 A.
(b) For the geyser, I = 2000/220 ≈ **9.1 A**, which is above 5 A, so the fuse wire heats up, melts and breaks the circuit.

(c) The fuse protects appliances and wiring from overloading and short circuits. The earth wire joins the metal body of an appliance to the ground, so any leakage current flows to earth and does not give a shock.

qa.q: Explain the working of an electric generator, including the role of slip rings and the commutator.
a: A coil is rotated mechanically in a magnetic field, so the magnetic flux linked with it keeps changing and an induced current is produced (electromagnetic induction).
The direction of the induced current reverses every half rotation, which is found by Fleming's right-hand rule.
In an AC generator two slip rings keep the coil connected to the external circuit without reversing the connections, so the output is alternating current.
A DC generator replaces them with a split-ring commutator, which reverses the connection to the external circuit every half turn so the output flows in one direction.

qa.q: Describe a domestic electric circuit and explain the function of the earth wire and the fuse.
a: The supply has three wires: **live** (red, at about 220 V), **neutral** (black, at zero potential) and **earth** (green).

Appliances are connected **in parallel** so that each receives the full supply voltage, each has its own switch, and the failure of one does not affect the others. Separate **15 A** and **5 A** circuits are provided for heavy and light appliances.

**Earth wire:** the metallic body of an appliance is connected to a metal plate buried in the earth, so if the live wire touches the body the leakage current flows safely into the ground instead of through a person — preventing a fatal shock.

**Fuse:** a short piece of wire of low melting point connected **in series** with the appliance. If the current exceeds the safe value, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, protecting the appliance from damage due to overloading or short circuiting.

qa.q: Describe the magnetic field produced by a current-carrying solenoid and explain how an electromagnet is made from it.
a: A solenoid is a coil of many closely wound circular turns of insulated copper wire.
The field lines inside the solenoid are parallel straight lines, so the field there is uniform; outside, the pattern is like that of a bar magnet.
One end of the solenoid behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
If a piece of soft iron is placed inside the coil, the strong field magnetises it, and the combination is an **electromagnet**.
It is a temporary magnet: it is magnetised only while the current flows. It is used in cranes for lifting iron, in electric bells and in MRI machines.

mcq.q: The direction of the magnetic field produced by a straight current-carrying wire is given by: (a) Fleming's left-hand rule (b) Fleming's right-hand rule (c) the right-hand thumb rule (d) Lenz's law
mcq.a: **(c) the right-hand thumb rule** — hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines.

mcq.q: The essential difference between an AC generator and a DC generator is: (a) AC generator has an electromagnet (b) DC generator has a commutator (c) AC generator has slip rings while DC generator has a commutator (d) AC generator produces more power
mcq.a: **(c).** The slip rings of an AC generator allow the output to reverse, while the split-ring commutator of a DC generator keeps the external current in one direction.

mcq.q: The frequency of AC supply in India is 50 Hz. The direction of the current changes: (a) 50 times per second (b) 100 times per second (c) 25 times per second (d) 200 times per second
mcq.a: **(b) 100 times per second** — the direction reverses twice in each cycle.

mcq.q: Outside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run: (a) from the south pole to the north pole  (b) in straight lines parallel to the axis only  (c) from the centre to both poles  (d) from the north pole to the south pole
mcq.a: **(d) from the north pole to the south pole.** By convention the field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet, and continue from south to north inside it.

mcq.q: A straight conductor carrying current is placed in a magnetic field. The force on it is greatest when the current is: (a) parallel to the field  (b) at 45° to the field  (c) zero  (d) perpendicular to the field
mcq.a: **(d) perpendicular to the field.** The force F = BIl sin θ is maximum at θ = 90°, and zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

mcq.q: The magnetic field lines inside a long current-carrying solenoid are: (a) concentric circles  (b) parallel straight lines  (c) diverging curves  (d) absent
mcq.a: **(b) parallel straight lines.** The field inside a solenoid is nearly uniform, like the field inside a bar magnet.

mcq.q: An electric motor converts: (a) electrical energy into mechanical energy  (b) mechanical energy into electrical energy  (c) heat into light  (d) chemical energy into sound
mcq.a: **(a) electrical energy into mechanical energy.** A generator does the reverse conversion.

mcq.q: The insulation on the earth wire in a domestic circuit is: (a) red  (b) black  (c) green  (d) blue
mcq.a: **(c) green.** Live is red or brown, neutral is black or blue, and earth is green or green-yellow.

mcq.q: The magnetic field at a point near a long straight current-carrying wire: (a) increases as you move away from the wire  (b) decreases as you move away from the wire  (c) does not depend on the current  (d) is zero everywhere around the wire
mcq.a: **(b) decreases as you move away from the wire.** The concentric field lines get farther apart with distance; the field is stronger for a larger current and closer to the wire.

mcq.q: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the: (a) induced current in a coil  (b) magnetic field due to a current  (c) force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field  (d) current produced by a generator
mcq.a: **(c) force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.** Forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force (motor). The right-hand rule is for generators.

mcq.q: The production of a current in a closed coil by a changing magnetic field is called: (a) electromagnetic induction  (b) magnetic effect of current  (c) electrolysis  (d) electrostatic induction
mcq.a: **(a) electromagnetic induction.** Faraday's discovery — the basis of the electric generator; the induced current direction is given by Fleming's right-hand rule.

trend: Fleming's two rules, the motor or generator working, and the domestic circuit with the earth wire and fuse rotate through the 3-mark slot; 'why field lines never intersect' is a standard 1-marker.
onepager: - Field lines: closed loops, N→S outside a magnet, never intersect.
- Left-hand rule = force on a conductor = motor. Right-hand rule = induced current = generator.
- Split ring reverses current each half rotation; AC 50 Hz reverses 100 times a second.
- Domestic: live 220 V, neutral 0 V, earth green; fuse in series, low melting point.
task: Build a simple electromagnet: wind 40 turns of insulated copper wire around an iron nail, connect it to two cells in series with a switch, and test how many pins it picks up. Then double the number of turns and repeat — the number of pins picked up shows that the field strength depends on the number of turns and the current.
steps: 1. Apply **Maxwell's right-hand thumb rule** to fix the direction of the field: thumb along the current, fingers curl along the field lines.
2. For the force on a conductor, use **Fleming's left-hand rule** (left hand for the motor effect): first finger field, second finger current, thumb force — all three mutually perpendicular.
3. For an induced current, switch to **Fleming's right-hand rule** (right hand for the generator effect) and state Faraday's law: the induced current is largest when the magnet or coil moves fast.

4. Finish with the **device and its safety part** — an electric motor uses a commutator to reverse current every half turn; domestic circuits use a fuse or MCB in the live wire, and earthing on the metal body of the appliance.

title: Our Environment
short: Food chains, the 10% law, ozone depletion and waste management.
lede: Five marks for an afternoon of study. The best marks-per-hour in the whole paper — do not leave it to the last day.
lens: **3–5 marks.** A food-chain question with the 10% energy calculation, one on ozone depletion, and one on biodegradable waste or the two environmental problems.
Case-based questions give a food chain with an energy value at one level and ask you to work out the others.
concepts: **1. Ecosystem.** All the living organisms (**biotic**) in an area together with the non-living (**abiotic**) components — temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals — form an ecosystem. **Producers** (green plants and blue-green algae) make their own food; **consumers** depend on them (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, parasites); **decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil. A pond and a forest are natural ecosystems; a crop field and an aquarium are artificial ones.

**2. Food chain and trophic levels.** A **food chain** shows who eats whom for the transfer of food energy: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk. Each step is a **trophic level**; producers occupy the first level. Energy flow in a food chain is always **unidirectional** — it passes from one level to the next and is never returned to the sun. A **food web** is a network of interconnected food chains.

**3. The 10% law.** Only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the remaining 90% is lost as heat, used in metabolism, or left in undigested matter. So if producers have 10,000 J, the herbivore gets 1,000 J, the next level 100 J, and the top carnivore only 10 J. This is why food chains rarely have more than four levels, and why a vegetarian diet supports a larger population.

**4. Biological magnification.** Harmful chemicals such as DDT and mercury are non-biodegradable and accumulate at **each** trophic level, so their concentration is **maximum in the top carnivore** — including human beings, who sit at the top of many food chains.

**5. Ozone layer depletion.** Ozone (O3) in the upper atmosphere shields the earth from harmful **ultraviolet radiation**. **Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**, used in refrigerators and air conditioners and in fire extinguishers, destroy ozone molecules, thinning the layer. Increased UV causes **skin cancer** and damage to crops and marine life. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** froze CFC production at 1986 levels to protect the ozone layer.

**6. Waste management.** **Biodegradable** waste (paper, vegetable peels, wood) is broken down by decomposers; **non-biodegradable** waste (plastic, glass, DDT, aluminium) is not. Problems caused by non-biodegradable waste: it does not decompose, pollutes soil and water, blocks drainage, and can enter food chains and biomagnify. Even biodegradable waste in excess causes foul smell, breeds mosquitoes and disease, and produces gases. **Methods of disposal:** segregating waste, **recycling** (paper, plastic, glass, metal), **composting and vermicomposting**, **sewage treatment** before releasing water into rivers, and burying waste in sanitary landfills. The **5 R's**: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle.
formulas: Energy at level n+1 = 10% of energy at level n
O3 formation: O2 + O →(UV) O3 ;  O3 + CFC → destruction of ozone
tricks: - **10% calculation:** move the decimal one place to the left at each level going up, and one place to the right going down.
- **Biomagnification = maximum at the top.** If the question asks which organism has the highest concentration, pick the top carnivore.
- **Biodegradable vs non-biodegradable** is decided by whether **micro-organisms can break it down** — not by whether it looks natural.
mistakes: - Drawing arrows in a food chain from predator to prey. Arrows always point **toward** the organism that eats — i.e. in the direction of **energy flow**.
- Applying 10% in the wrong direction. Going **down** the chain, multiply by 10 at each step, not by 0.1.
- Saying the ozone layer protects us from infrared radiation. It is **ultraviolet** radiation.
- Confusing **biological magnification** with **biodegradability** — they are different concepts entirely.

qa.q: Name the organisms that always occupy the first trophic level of a food chain, and define an ecosystem.
qa.a: Green plants and blue-green algae (producers). An ecosystem is a self-sustaining system in which all the living organisms of an area interact with each other and with the non-living (abiotic) components such as soil, water and air.

qa.q: Why are some substances biodegradable and some non-biodegradable?
qa.a: Because micro-organisms such as bacteria and fungi produce enzymes that can break down only certain substances like paper, wood and vegetable waste. Substances such as plastic, glass and DDT cannot be acted upon by these enzymes, so they remain in the environment for a very long time and are called non-biodegradable.

qa.q: Suggest two ways to reduce the problem of waste disposal.
qa.a: Segregate waste at the source and send biodegradable waste for composting or vermicomposting; and practise the 5 R's — refuse what is unnecessary, reduce consumption, reuse containers, repurpose items, and recycle paper, plastic, glass and metal.

qa.q: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web.
qa.a: A food chain is a single linear sequence showing who eats whom, for example grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. A food web is a network of many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem; because each organism can feed at more than one level, the web is far more stable than a single chain.

qa.q: In a food chain, if 10,000 joules of solar energy is available to the producers, how much energy will be available to the secondary consumer?
a: Producers convert about 1% of the solar energy into food energy, but taking 10,000 J as the energy **in the producers**: primary consumer receives 10% = **1,000 J**.
Secondary consumer receives 10% of 1,000 J = **100 J**.

qa.q: What is ozone? How is it formed, and why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern?
a: Ozone is a molecule of oxygen with three atoms, O3, found in the upper atmosphere.
**Formation:** ultraviolet radiation splits an oxygen molecule into free oxygen atoms, O2 →(UV) 2O; each free atom combines with an oxygen molecule to form ozone, O + O2 → O3.

**Concern:** the ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun. Its depletion, caused mainly by CFCs from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosols, allows more UV to reach the earth, causing skin cancer, damage to the eyes, reduced crop yields and harm to marine organisms. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 froze CFC production to protect it.

qa.q: A student draws the food chain as Hawk → Snake → Frog → Grasshopper → Grass. What is wrong? Redraw it correctly and name the trophic levels.
a: An arrow shows the direction of energy flow, from the food **to** the organism that eats it. The student’s arrows point from predator to prey.
Correct chain: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk.
Trophic levels: grass is the producer (1st); grasshopper the primary consumer (2nd); frog the secondary consumer (3rd); snake the tertiary consumer (4th); hawk the top consumer (5th).

qa.q: Explain the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
a: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down the dead bodies of plants and animals and their wastes into simple inorganic substances.
These substances — mineral salts, carbon dioxide and water — go back into the soil and air and are reused by the producers.
They also clean up the environment. Without decomposers nutrients would stay locked in dead matter and the cycling of matter would stop.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

In a grassland food chain, the producers capture 20,000 J of energy.

(a) How much energy reaches the herbivores?
(b) How much energy reaches the carnivores that eat the herbivores?
(c) Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
a: (a) By the 10% law, herbivores get 10% of 20,000 J = **2,000 J**.
(b) The carnivores get 10% of 2,000 J = **200 J**.
(c) About 90% of the energy at each level is lost as heat in life processes, so very little is left to support more levels.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A sealed glass jar contains water, a few water plants, small fish and snails, and some soil at the bottom. It is kept in sunlight.

(a) Name the producers, consumers and decomposers in the jar.
(b) What is the role of sunlight?
(c) What would happen if the jar were kept in the dark for a long time?
a: (a) Producers: the water plants (and algae); consumers: the fish and snails; decomposers: the bacteria and fungi in the water and soil.
(b) Sunlight is the source of energy: the plants use it for photosynthesis, which provides food and oxygen for the other organisms.
(c) Without light, the plants could not photosynthesise, so food and oxygen would run out and the organisms would die.

qa.q: A village panchayat plans to burn its collected plastic waste in the open. Advise them, giving reasons from what you have studied about ecosystems.
a: Open burning of plastic releases poisonous gases such as hydrogen chloride and dioxins into the air, harming people, animals and crops.
Plastics are non-biodegradable, so if they are buried or dumped they persist in the soil for decades and choke drains and the guts of animals.
Better: segregate waste at source, send recyclable plastic for recycling, compost the biodegradable fraction, and replace single-use plastic with cloth or paper bags.
This keeps harmful chemicals out of the soil and water, so they cannot enter food chains and build up by biological magnification.

qa.q: What is biological magnification? Will the level of magnification be different at different levels of the ecosystem?
a: Biological magnification is the progressive increase in the concentration of non-biodegradable harmful chemicals at successive trophic levels of a food chain.

Yes, the level differs. Because these chemicals are not metabolised or excreted, they pass on to the next level, and the amount of food consumed at each level is large, so the concentration keeps increasing.

**Example:** DDT sprayed on crops is absorbed by plants; grasshoppers eating many plants accumulate more; frogs eating many grasshoppers more still; and hawks at the top accumulate the highest concentration. Human beings, being at the top of many food chains, are among the most affected.

qa.q: What is a trophic level? Explain the flow of energy in an ecosystem and why it is unidirectional.
a: A trophic level is a step in a food chain, for example producers, herbivores and carnivores.
The ultimate source of energy is the Sun; producers capture it through photosynthesis and pass it on when eaten.
At each step only about 10% of the energy is passed on to the next level (the 10% law); the rest is lost as heat in respiration and other life processes.
The energy lost as heat cannot be used again by the producers, so energy flows in **one direction only**, from the Sun to producers to consumers.
Because so little energy remains, food chains are short, and plants always occupy the first level.

mcq.q: In the food chain Grass → Deer → Lion, if 10,000 J of energy is available to the grass, the energy available to the lion is: (a) 1000 J (b) 100 J (c) 10 J (d) 1 J
mcq.a: **(b) 100 J.** Grass 10,000 J → deer 1,000 J → lion 100 J (10% at each transfer).

mcq.q: The depletion of the ozone layer is mainly caused by: (a) CO2 (b) CFCs (c) methane (d) SO2
mcq.a: **(b) CFCs** — chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerators, air conditioners and fire extinguishers destroy ozone molecules.

mcq.q: Which of the following groups contains only biodegradable substances? (a) paper, plastic, wood (b) vegetable peels, paper, lime juice (c) glass, wood, plastic (d) lime juice, grass, aluminium foil
mcq.a: **(b)** — all three are broken down by the action of micro-organisms.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a non-biodegradable waste? (a) a plastic bag (b) vegetable peelings (c) a paper bag (d) a cotton cloth
mcq.a: **(a) a plastic bag.** Microorganisms cannot break down plastics, so they persist in the environment for a very long time.

mcq.q: In the food chain Plant → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake, the secondary consumer is the: (a) grasshopper (b) snake (c) plant (d) frog
mcq.a: **(d) frog.** The grasshopper is the primary consumer and the frog, which eats it, is the secondary consumer.

mcq.q: The ‘10% law’ in an ecosystem describes the transfer of: (a) energy  (b) water  (c) minerals  (d) oxygen
mcq.a: **(a) energy.** Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is stored in the next; the rest is lost as heat and in life processes.

mcq.q: Which of these is a renewable resource? (a) coal  (b) petroleum  (c) sunlight  (d) natural gas
mcq.a: **(c) sunlight.** Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels that take millions of years to form.

mcq.q: The ozone layer is being depleted mainly by: (a) CFCs  (b) methane  (c) nitrogen fertilisers  (d) carbon monoxide
mcq.a: **(a) CFCs.** Chlorofluorocarbons from refrigerants and aerosol sprays release chlorine atoms that destroy ozone molecules.

trend: One food chain with a 10% energy calculation is asked almost every year, alternating with ozone depletion or biodegradable vs non-biodegradable waste.
onepager: - Food chain arrows point in the direction of energy flow; producers are always the first trophic level.
- 10% law: only about 10% of energy transfers upward, so chains rarely exceed four levels.
- Biological magnification is maximum in the top carnivore (e.g. hawks, human beings).
- O3 shields UV; CFCs deplete it; Montreal Protocol 1987 froze CFC production.
- 5 R's: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle.
task: Survey your own household waste for three days and sort it into biodegradable and non-biodegradable. Weigh or count each group, then list two things you could refuse or reuse that would remove the largest share of the non-biodegradable waste from the bin.
steps: 1. Identify the level the question is set at: **ecosystem components** (biotic and abiotic), a **food chain or web**, or **waste management**.

2. For a food chain, write the arrow as **'is eaten by'** and place the producer first. If a pesticide or energy question follows, apply the **10 per cent law** at each trophic level and quote biological magnification for harmful chemicals.
3. For depletion or pollution, name the **cause, the mechanism and one remedy** — for example, CFCs break ozone, and the remedy was to phase them out under the Montreal Protocol.
4. Close with the **action** that is asked for: reduce, reuse, recycle (with 'refuse' and 'rethink' if the question wants the full five Rs), and segregate biodegradable from non-biodegradable waste.
